levels.title: Identify Spreadsheet Rows and Columns
levels.objective: Distinguish headers, records, cells and data types in an order sheet.
levels.teaching: A column stores one field, a row stores one complete record, and a cell names one intersection. Reliable sheets use a unique header row.

challenges.prompt: In a bookshop workbook A1=Order ID, B1=Date, C1=Amount. What does C4 refer to?

options.b: The amount stored in row four

challenges.feedback: The letter C identifies the Amount column; 4 identifies the fourth row. C4 is one amount cell.

challenges.prompt: A colleague says 'the total is wrong in row 12.' Which reference helps you find the amount without changing another field?

options.a: Look at B12 because B always means amount
options.b: Look at the entire sheet and delete row 12
options.c: Check which column has the Amount header, then inspect its row-12 cell

challenges.feedback: Columns must be identified by their actual headers before interpreting a row number.

challenges.prompt: In a one-record-per-row order sheet, each row below the header should describe one order, not mix several orders in one cell.
challenges.feedback: Keeping one order per row makes sorting and formulas reliable; a header row is not an order.

levels.title: Set Up a Clean Data Table
levels.objective: Choose useful column names and one-record-per-row structure.
levels.teaching: A usable transaction table needs one header per field, consistent values and a stable identifier. Avoid merged cells and repeated header rows inside data.

challenges.prompt: You are designing an orders table. Which header set supports filtering and totals?

options.b: Order ID, Order Date, Item, Quantity, Unit Price
options.c: Order details including the date, product and everything else

challenges.feedback: Separate date, quantity and unit price fields allow meaningful formulas and filtering.

challenges.prompt: A shop records 'Order 501, two red bags, PKR 2,000' as one merged cell. What is the best redesign?

options.a: Separate ID, item, quantity and unit price into dedicated columns
options.b: Keep merged cells but color them yellow
options.c: Use a new worksheet for each order

challenges.feedback: Separate fields make calculations, validation and sorting possible without extracting values from prose.

challenges.prompt: Repeating a header row after every five orders inside one data range improves spreadsheet filtering.
challenges.feedback: Repeated headers become data records and disrupt filters. Use frozen headers or a formatted table instead.

levels.title: Keep Dates, Money and Numbers Consistent
levels.objective: Spot data types that distort financial summaries.
levels.teaching: A cell that looks like a number may actually be text. Store numeric amounts numerically and use number formatting for currency; choose a consistent date convention.

challenges.prompt: A SUM of four prices ignores 'PKR 850' typed as text in one cell. What should change?

options.a: Replace the amount with a numeric 850 and format the cell as PKR
options.b: Add the word total next to every price
options.c: Convert the entire sheet to plain text

challenges.feedback: Numbers must remain numeric for arithmetic; the PKR label belongs in formatting.

challenges.prompt: Two dates appear as 03/04/2026 and 2026-04-03. Your team uses day-month-year. How should you avoid confusing the order dates?

options.b: Record dates consistently with a stated convention, preferably as actual date values
options.c: Sort both as raw text and trust the result

challenges.feedback: Ambiguous date strings can invert day and month and break accurate chronological reports.

challenges.prompt: The value 1,200 entered as text with an apostrophe will always behave exactly like numeric 1200 in SUM calculations.
challenges.feedback: Text and numeric values can look identical but may behave differently in formulas and sorting.

levels.title: Find Missing and Duplicate Records
levels.objective: Identify blanks, duplicates and legitimate repeated orders.
levels.teaching: Duplicate detection needs a reliable key such as Order ID. Two similar purchases can be real separate orders; blank fields require verification instead of assumptions.

challenges.prompt: Order ID 741 occurs twice with identical date, item, quantity and amount. What should you do before removing either row?

options.b: Confirm whether the two rows represent one event using the source order log
options.c: Keep both because duplicates are never mistakes

challenges.feedback: Even a perfect-looking duplicate needs comparison with source records before deletion.

challenges.prompt: Order 782 and 783 have the same customer and total, but different order IDs and timestamps. What is the safest interpretation?

options.a: Keep both as potentially legitimate separate orders pending evidence
options.b: Merge them because the totals match
options.c: Set the customer field to blank on one record

challenges.feedback: Matching customer and total are not sufficient to establish a duplicate transaction.

challenges.prompt: A blank delivery date should be filled with today's date without checking the shipment record.
challenges.feedback: Inventing dates contaminates operational reports; missing data should be marked and verified.

levels.title: Sort, Filter and Inspect Data
levels.objective: Use filters to answer a business question without destroying records.
levels.teaching: Filtering hides unmatched records without deleting them. Sort the complete table range to preserve the relationship between order IDs and amounts.

challenges.prompt: How do you show only orders marked 'Pending' while retaining all completed orders?

options.b: Apply a filter on the Status column for Pending

challenges.feedback: Filters change the visible view, not the underlying records.

challenges.prompt: Someone sorts only the Amount cells, leaving Order ID and customer columns in place. What problem results?

options.a: The spreadsheet improves because amounts are grouped
options.c: Amounts may be attached to the wrong orders

challenges.feedback: Sort the whole table so each record stays together across all columns.

challenges.prompt: After a filter hides 18 completed orders, those orders are permanently removed from the spreadsheet.
challenges.feedback: Filters only hide rows until the filter is cleared; deleting rows is a separate action.

levels.title: Checkpoint: Clean Sample Orders
levels.objective: Correct a 25-row synthetic order dataset using a documented checklist.
levels.teaching: A cleaning pass should verify headers, IDs, numeric fields, dates and missing values, then reconcile record counts against the source rather than silently guessing.

challenges.prompt: A synthetic 25-row order file has one repeated Order ID, two missing quantities and three currency strings. Which check should come before final totals?

options.a: Verify the duplicate and missing quantities against source records, then convert text amounts safely
options.b: Delete all rows with any unusual value
options.c: Format every column red and publish the total

challenges.feedback: Quality control comes before arithmetic; unresolved source discrepancies must be reported.

challenges.prompt: A cleaned file now has 24 rows. The source log shows 25 actual orders and one shared customer name. What should you check?

options.a: Assume the customer repeated because data is broken
options.b: Reconcile every original Order ID and restore any distinct order incorrectly removed
options.c: Add an invented order to make the count 25

challenges.feedback: Record count must be reconciled to unique source order IDs, not guessed from customer names.

challenges.prompt: A cleaning report should distinguish corrections confirmed by a source from unresolved blanks that still need attention.
challenges.feedback: A transparent audit separates verified repairs from uncertainties so downstream analysis is trustworthy.
